summary.younger: God made everything out of nothing, and he made people to know him and to take care of his world.
summary.older: Before anything else, there is God. He speaks the world into being, calls it good, and makes people in his image to care for it under him.

summary.younger: The first people did not trust God and did what he told them not to do. Sin and sadness came into the world, but God kept caring for them.
summary.older: Adam and Eve reach for what God withheld, and the damage spreads: shame, blame, murder, the flood, a tower built to reach the sky. God judges, and he keeps showing mercy.

summary.younger: God chose Abraham and promised him a family as many as the stars, a land to live in, and a blessing for the whole world.
summary.older: God answers a scattered world by calling one man and making him a promise: a people, a land, and a blessing that will reach every family on earth.

summary.younger: God's people were slaves in Egypt. God set them free on the night of the Passover and led them through the sea.
summary.older: Abraham's family has become a nation of slaves. God hears them, sends Moses, spares them by the blood of a lamb, and opens a road through the sea.

summary.younger: At a mountain called Sinai, God gave his people his good laws and told them to build a tent where he would live among them.
summary.older: Rescued people are given a way to live. At Sinai God makes a covenant with Israel, gives the law, and has them build the tabernacle so that he can dwell among them.

summary.younger: God brought his people into the land he had promised. They kept forgetting him, and God kept sending leaders to rescue them.
summary.older: God keeps his word and gives the land. Then a cycle begins: the people turn away, trouble comes, they cry out, God sends a judge. Each time round it gets worse.

stops.title: The Kingdom
stops.range: 1 Samuel to 1 Kings 11, and the Psalms

summary.younger: God gave Israel kings. The greatest was David, a shepherd boy, and God promised that a king from his family would rule for ever.
summary.older: Israel asks for a king. Saul fails; David loves God and fails badly too; God promises him a son whose kingdom will never end. Solomon builds the temple.

stops.title: The Prophets and Exile
stops.range: 1 Kings 12 to 2 Kings 25, and the Prophets

summary.younger: The people stopped listening to God. Prophets warned them, but they would not turn back, and they were taken far from home.
summary.older: The kingdom splits, its kings lead the people to idols, and God sends prophets to call them back. They will not come. Assyria takes the north and Babylon burns Jerusalem, yet the prophets promise a new covenant and a coming king.

summary.younger: God brought some of his people home. They rebuilt the temple and the city walls, and then they waited a long time for God's promised king.
summary.older: Some exiles come home under Persian rule and rebuild the temple and the walls, but no son of David sits on the throne. The Old Testament ends looking ahead, and roughly four centuries pass before the next page.

summary.younger: God the Son was born as a baby named Jesus. He healed people, taught about God's kingdom, and showed what God is like.
summary.older: God keeps his promises in person. Jesus, born of Mary, announces that God's kingdom has come near, heals and forgives, calls twelve disciples, and speaks with an authority that belongs to God alone.

stops.title: The Cross and the Empty Tomb

summary.younger: Jesus died on a cross to take away the sin of the world. On the third day God raised him from the dead. He is alive.
summary.older: Jesus dies on a Roman cross at Passover, carrying the sin of the world, and on the third day God raises him bodily from the dead.

summary.younger: Jesus went back to his Father and sent the Holy Spirit. His followers told the good news about Jesus to people everywhere.
summary.older: Fifty days after Passover the Spirit comes. The church begins in Jerusalem and spreads, Jews and Gentiles together, until the news of Jesus reaches Rome.

stops.title: The New Creation
stops.range: Revelation 21 to 22, with 1 Corinthians 15 and Romans 8

summary.younger: One day Jesus will come back and make everything new. God will live with his people, and there will be no more crying or pain.
summary.older: The story ends where it began, with God and his people together, in a garden that has become a city. Jesus returns, death is undone, and God makes his home with people for ever.

line.younger: From the first page to the last, God wants to live with his people. Follow the places where he makes his home.
line.older: The whole Bible can be read as one long answer to a question: can God live with his people? Watch where he dwells move from a garden to a tent, a temple, a person, a people, and a whole new world.

key.apart: The closeness is lost, or still waited for

creation.line: God planted a garden and put the people he made there, close to him.

fall.line: The man and the woman hid from God among the trees, and they were sent out of the garden.

abraham.line: God came to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Jacob woke from a dream and said the LORD was in that place.

rescue.line: God went ahead of his people in a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night.

sinai.line: God told Israel to build a tent, the tabernacle, so that he could dwell among them, and his glory filled it.

land.line: In the land, the tent of meeting was set up at Shiloh, among the tribes.

kingdom.line: Solomon built the temple in Jerusalem, and the cloud of God's glory filled it.

exile.line: The prophet Ezekiel saw God's glory leave the temple before Babylon destroyed it.

return.line: The people rebuilt the temple, and God promised that one day he would fill it with glory.

jesus.line: Jesus is God with us. The Word became flesh and made his dwelling among us.

cross.line: When Jesus died, the curtain that closed off the most holy place in the temple tore from top to bottom.

church.line: God's Spirit came to live in his people. Paul tells the church that it is now God's temple.

new-creation.line: At the end, God's dwelling place is with people, and he lives with them for ever.

line.younger: God makes promises to his people, and he always keeps them.
line.older: God binds himself to people by covenant: with Noah, Abraham, Israel at Sinai and David, and at last the new covenant in Jesus.

line.younger: Again and again a lamb dies in the place of someone else, until Jesus, the Lamb of God.
line.older: Sacrifice runs from the garden to the cross: a substitute, a covering, a price paid by another.

line.younger: God's people wait for a good king, and Jesus is that king.
line.older: People made to rule under God want to rule without him. The story looks for the true king, the son of David, who reigns by serving.

key.reigns: God's rule is shown, or his king is on the throne
key.waited: The king is promised, or the throne stands empty

creation.line: God made people in his image to rule over his world under him, caring for it as he would.

fall.line: People grabbed at ruling without God. Then God promised that the woman's seed would crush the serpent's head.

abraham.line: God promised Abraham, “kings will descend from you.”

rescue.line: At the sea God showed who really rules, and Moses and Israel sang, “The LORD will reign forever and ever!”

sinai.line: At Sinai, God, Israel's true king, made his people “a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.”

land.line: Judges ends sadly: “In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in his own eyes.”

kingdom.line: God promised David a son whose kingdom would last: “your throne will be established forever.”

exile.line: When Babylon took Jerusalem, David's throne was lost. Isaiah had promised a child who “will reign on the throne of David.”

return.line: The people came home, but no son of David sat on the throne. Zechariah told them, “See, your King comes to you.”

jesus.line: Jesus announced that “the kingdom of God is near,” and Peter said he was the Christ, the promised king.

cross.line: The soldiers crowned Jesus with thorns, and the charge over the cross read “THE KING OF THE JEWS.” On the third day God raised him.

church.line: God seated the risen Jesus at his right hand and made him “head over everything for the church,” which is his body.

new-creation.line: At the end, “The throne of God and of the Lamb will be within the city,” and his people reign with him for ever.

line.younger: God's plan was always for people from every country.
line.older: Through Abraham's family God means to bless all the families of the earth, and the last pages show people from every nation together.

cards.title: The Bible
cards.pictureLabel: An open Bible on a table under an arched window.

statement.younger: The Bible is God's true Word. God gave it through many writers over a very long time, and it tells one big story, about Jesus saving us.
statement.older: The Bible is sixty-six books written by many people over many centuries, and through those human writers God himself speaks. It is God-breathed, true in all it teaches, and Jesus is its center: he said the Scriptures testify about him.

quote.text: All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness, so that the man of God may be complete, fully equipped for every good work.

question.ask: How can a book written by people be God's Word?
question.younger: God used real people, with their own words and their own ways of writing. The Holy Spirit carried them along, so that what they wrote is what God wanted to say.
question.older: Christians do not say the writers took dictation. Luke says he carefully investigated everything before he wrote (Luke 1:3). They say God was at work in the whole of it, so that men “spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit” (2 Peter 1:21). That is a claim to weigh, not to swallow, and the questions about how the books were copied and collected are fair ones.

cards.title: Jesus, God and man
cards.pictureLabel: A manger full of straw in a stable at night, under one bright star.

statement.younger: Jesus is God the Son. He became a real man, born as a baby, so that he could save us. He is fully God and fully man.
statement.older: Jesus is one person who is truly God and truly man; the church confessed it in those words at the Council of Chalcedon in 451. He was with God and was God from the beginning, and he became flesh: he grew tired, he wept, he died. Only someone who is both could bring God and people back together.

quote.text: The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us. We have seen His glory, the glory of the one and only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth.

question.ask: If Jesus is God, who was he praying to?
question.younger: He was praying to God the Father. There is one God, who is the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. The Son loves to talk with the Father.
question.older: To God the Father. Christians confess one God in three persons: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Jesus praying shows that the Son and the Father are two persons, not that Jesus is less than God. The same Gospel that shows him praying ends with Thomas calling him “My Lord and my God” (John 20:28).
